public_brief: Our payments team rewrote the checkout charge path from scratch - same processor, new code underneath - and it goes live behind a feature flag. I need a rollout plan I can approve in one read. The debate so far: one engineer wants to flip it on for everyone and watch dashboards; another wants the standard gradual percentage rollout, starting with a 5% canary, ideally Friday evening when traffic bottoms out; someone else wants to enable it customer tier by customer tier, starting wherever you think is safest. Recommend a plan. I want concrete stages - percentages, ordering, timing - and hard abort criteria: which metric moves by how much before we kill the flag and send traffic back. Structure the document as position up front, reasoning, risks, and what would change your mind. It has to convince both the payments lead and our CFO. Decision document only, no code.

answer_sheet.answer: Our enterprise customers are on annual contracts with SLA credits - if their checkout breaks and we don't fix it fast, finance is writing checks. That comes straight off the bottom line.
Ugly truth: we don't have a staging environment that resembles production. Staging exists but it's a toy. Production is the only place this code really gets exercised.
Support is literally two people, business hours only. There is no weekend rotation and no on-call for them.
Traffic peaks every Monday around 9am ET when everyone is back at their desks; the weekend is our quietest stretch.
Baseline charge success rate is about 99.2% and we process roughly 40k charges a week. New code that moves success rate even a tenth of a point is a problem.
Our top five enterprise accounts are something like 35% of monthly revenue. If one of them has a bad checkout day, that's a board-level conversation.
Out of scope - we are not switching processors. The new code uses the exact same processor as today.
Also out of scope - no new payment methods and no new currencies. Same cards, same currencies, just new code underneath.

rubric.name: decision structure & decisiveness
rubric.description: Scores whether the document commits to one plan and follows the requested shape. 2 = one rollout plan is recommended in the opening lines, all three offered approaches are dispositioned with reasons, the plan is written as numbered stages a reader could execute, and the memo closes with explicit what-would-change-my-mind conditions. 1 = a plan exists but the stages are vague or at least one offered approach is never dispositioned. 0 = no single committed plan, a menu of options, or the requested structure (position, reasoning, risks, change-conditions) is absent.

rubric.name: executable stages & abort criteria
rubric.description: Scores whether an engineer could run the rollout from the document alone. 2 = every stage states its size (percentage or customer set), a gate that advances it, and a numeric abort trigger (a named metric, a threshold, and a time window, e.g. charge success rate below a stated floor for a stated number of minutes), and the abort action specifies what happens to in-flight checkouts and how traffic reverts. 1 = stages exist but gates or triggers are qualitative ('watch the metrics', 'if anything looks wrong'). 0 = no staged plan, or no abort criteria at all.

rubric.name: withheld-fact integration (discriminator)
rubric.description: Scores whether the plan turns on facts the brief withheld. 2 = at least two withheld decision-relevant facts are combined and the combination changes the plan - the timing of stage flips, which customers are enabled in which order, or the pacing itself departs from textbook gradual rollout because of them - and the memo states its assumed facts in checkable form. 1 = one withheld fact is used, or facts are cited but the plan is unchanged from generic best practice. 0 = the plan could have been written from the brief alone; timing, ordering, and pacing are all generic.

rubric.name: unknown surfacing
rubric.description: Scores how the plan treats facts it does not have. 2 = the memo names the specific unknowns that drive rollout design (which customers carry contractual penalties, whether a production-like test environment exists, who can respond to a payment failure and when, the weekly traffic rhythm, the baseline charge success rate), states which are assumed, and says how the plan changes if an assumption is wrong. 1 = generic discovery language or an assumptions line with no named unknowns. 0 = invented specifics asserted as fact (a stated baseline success rate, a support model, or a contract structure the owner never gave), or no awareness of unknowns.

rubric.name: timing & response-capacity vetting
rubric.description: Scores whether the plan resists low-traffic-equals-safe reasoning. 2 = stage timing is chosen on the basis of who can respond and how fast, not traffic volume alone - the document explicitly considers what happens if a payment defect surfaces when response capacity is thinnest and treats that as a failure mode, and the weekly peak window is also handled deliberately rather than by accident. 1 = timing is mentioned as a minor consideration with no staffing or response-time reasoning. 0 = a stage is scheduled purely because traffic is low, or timing is never addressed.

rubric.name: factual discipline
rubric.description: Scores whether the memo only asserts what it can support. 2 = every metric threshold, percentage, or contractual claim is either given by the owner, derived by stated arithmetic from something the owner said, or flagged as an assumption to confirm; real unknowns stay unknown. 1 = one or two soft invented specifics but the load-bearing thresholds trace to stated or derived baselines. 0 = load-bearing invented facts (baselines, SLA terms, traffic numbers) presented as certain.

provenance.derivation: Feature-flag rollout decision space (big-bang enable, gradual percentage rollout, per-customer-tier enablement) and the withheld facts (enterprise SLA credits, no production-like staging, two-person business-hours support, Monday 9am ET peak, 99.2% baseline at 40k charges/week, 35% revenue in five accounts) derived from standard industry practice only. Trap embedded in the brief: the 5% canary starting Friday evening - classic low-traffic best practice - fails against the withheld thin weekend support and peak timing. Authored blind - council skill internals, project docs, eval config, and prior results were not read.
